name: Embrace
label: Dischord
lede: Nine shows in under a year, one album released after the band was already gone, and the moment Ian MacKaye slowed hardcore down to hear what else it could say.

eras.title: Minor Threat's singer, Faith's band
eras.text: Two years after Minor Threat, Ian MacKaye wanted out of the violence that had swallowed hardcore shows, not out of punk. Embrace kept the fire but slowed the tempo, and turned the songs toward greed, self-delusion and the scene itself, right as Revolution Summer was remaking D.C.

years.h: Ian MacKaye joins three ex-members of Faith
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] joins [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]], [[Chris Bald|0838359b-95a7-48e9-a9f6-0e8f40bb34d2]] and [[Ivor Hanson|a17981f7-ab3d-46dc-859a-582ac894cb20]], three ex-members of [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]], the band his brother [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]] had fronted. Hampton and Hanson go back even further, to [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

years.h: Embrace's first show: Food for Thought, Dupont Circle
years.p: Embrace debut at Food for Thought in Dupont Circle in the middle of Revolution Summer. MacKaye's new band is slower, more melodic and more inward than anything he'd fronted before.
years.xp:
AllMusic's line on them: the fire and passion of hardcore, albeit slower and more heartfelt. Dischord describes small rooms and a personal, introspective take on punk rock.

Across town, [[Rites of Spring|b2ff1a6d-9198-4646-b068-8965242d245b]] were pulling in the same direction. Between the two bands, D.C. hardcore was learning a new register.

eras.title: Nine shows and out
eras.text: Embrace finished their record and then simply stopped. By spring Ian MacKaye was in London recording as Egg Hunt with his old Minor Threat drummer Jeff Nelson, Michael Hampton was in One Last Wish with three ex-Rites of Spring members, and the Embrace album sat waiting.

years.p: Embrace's ninth show, at the 9:30 Club, is its last. AllMusic called the breakup unceremonious, and nobody in the band has given a reason on the record.
years.xp: Embrace's four members scattered fast. Michael Hampton went to [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]], Chris Bald to [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]], and Ivor Hanson would reunite with Hampton in Manifesto. Ian MacKaye tried a few things before landing on Fugazi.

years.h: Ian MacKaye and Jeff Nelson record as [[Egg Hunt|2d8d08d8-c1b1-4494-b299-32dd4a7f8dfe]] in London
years.p: Ian MacKaye and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] record four songs at Southern Records' Wood Green studio in England over Easter weekend and name the project Egg Hunt. Dischord calls it the last time the two recorded music together.

years.h: Michael Hampton joins three ex-Rites of Spring in One Last Wish
years.p: Guy Picciotto, Eddie Janney and Brendan Canty start One Last Wish with Michael Hampton on guitar.

years.h: MacKaye and Nelson try to make Egg Hunt a full band
years.p: Ian MacKaye and Jeff Nelson try to build a full Egg Hunt line-up with ex-members of [[Gray Matter|c9065214-ba09-4c2c-b341-35713b702264]]. In Dischord's words, it wasn't meant to be.

years.big: The scene had a new name for what they did. He didn't want it.
years.h: Brian Baker coins "emocore"; Ian MacKaye wants no part of it
years.p: Dag Nasty's Brian Baker told Parade in 2025 he made up "emocore" at a December 1985 show to mock Rites of Spring's set. The word stuck to Embrace too, and in 1986 MacKaye called it stupid.
years.xp:
Embrace, Dag Nasty and Rites of Spring shared the bill on December 4, 1985. Baker was MacKaye's old Minor Threat bandmate.

For MacKaye the point had been to strip away hardcore's posturing, not to start a subgenre. The label stuck anyway and outlived both bands by decades.

years.h: "Dance of Days" live at the 9:30 Club, 1986
yt: "Dance of Days" live at the 9:30 Club, 1986

eras.title: The record outlives the band
eras.text: Embrace's only album came out more than a year after the last show, from a band that no longer existed. By then Ian MacKaye had a new group, Fugazi, that would make Embrace's slower, searching sound the starting point for something much bigger.

years.h: Embrace's album comes out, a year after the band split
years.p: Recorded at Inner Ear from November 1985 to February 1986, Embrace's only album came out as Dischord No. 24 in September 1987. Critic Mark Jenkins heard sermons against greed, delusion and self-destruction.
years.xp:
[[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]] engineered the sessions in Arlington. [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]] of Rites of Spring plays guitar on one track and shares the production credit with the band and Ian MacKaye.

Fourteen songs, about 33 minutes. Jenkins credited Chris Bald with much of the words.

Trouser Press argued the strong, muscular instrumentals turned an okay mid-tempo punk LP into a great one.

Songs like Money and Last Song pointed straight at where Ian MacKaye was headed next, Fugazi.

years.h: Ian MacKaye's next band, Fugazi, plays its first show
years.p: [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] debut at the Wilson Center. Brendan Canty is on drums, and Guy Picciotto is singing with them within weeks: two of the Rites of Spring players Embrace had shared those 1985 bills with.

years.h: Michael Hampton and Ivor Hanson reunite in Manifesto
years.p: Embrace's guitarist and drummer, bandmates since SOA, reunite in Manifesto.

eras.title: Other bands' Embrace
eras.text: Embrace never reunited, but the record kept getting remade, remastered and covered. A younger generation of hardcore and pop-punk bands paid it back in the most D.C. way possible: a benefit.

years.h: Embrace's album on CD, with a new cover
years.p: Embrace's album arrives on CD and cassette with alternate cover art.

years.h: An Embrace tribute album benefits homeless shelters
years.p: Trustkill Records releases Land of Greed... World of Need, with [[Avail|d67ff511-57b8-4d02-94d3-6c6a331c2ae4]], [[Rancid|24f8d8a5-269b-475c-a1cb-792990b0b2ee]] and [[Lifetime|c9329809-8510-45b9-9202-5640398ddaee]] among the bands covering Embrace. Proceeds go to homeless shelters.

years.h: Embrace remastered, with two alternate takes
years.p: Chad Clark remasters Embrace's album at Silver Sonya, and alternate versions of Money and Dance of Days are added.

years.h: Embrace drummer Ivor Hanson writes a book about washing windows
years.p: Ivor Hanson publishes Life on the Ledge: Reflections of a New York City Window Cleaner, a memoir of his years washing windows high up on Manhattan buildings. Two Dollar Radio put it out.
After a red vinyl pressing in 2008, Embrace's LP is remastered by Jason Ward at Chicago Mastering Service.
